title: Love Your Neighbor
common: All five ask you to widen your circle of care beyond yourself — toward family, strangers and, in some, every living being.
differ: The reason given varies. The Torah and Quran present it as God's command; Jesus sums up 'the law and the prophets' with it; the Gita grounds it in seeing one Self in everyone; the Diamond Sutra goes further and asks you to drop the line between self and other altogether.
reflect: Whose 'neighbor' are you finding it hardest to be right now?

passages.quote: He who, through the likeness of the Self, O Arjuna, sees reality everywhere, be it pleasure or pain, is regarded as the highest Yogi.
Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.

However many living beings there are — born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture or by transformation; with form or without; with thought or without — I will lead them all to complete liberation. Yet when countless beings have been liberated, in truth no being has been liberated. Why? Because one who holds on to the idea of a self, a person, a being or a life is not a true bodhisattva.

And serve Allah. Ascribe no thing as partner unto Him. (Show) kindness unto parents, and unto near kindred, and orphans, and the needy, and unto the neighbour who is of kin (unto you) and the neighbour who is not of kin, and the fellow-traveller and the wayfarer and (the slaves) whom your right hands possess. Lo! Allah loveth not such as are proud and boastful
Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.

title: Everyone Is Equal
hook: Does status matter to the sacred?
common: Each text pushes back on ranking people by birth, tribe or status.
differ: The basis differs: shared memory of being strangers (Torah), unity in Christ (Bible), diversity created so people may know one another and judged only by conduct (Quran), the same Self in every creature (Gita), and a truth with 'no high and no low' (Diamond Sutra). Historically, each tradition has also lived with its own hierarchies — worth exploring honestly.
reflect: Where do you notice yourself ranking people without meaning to?

passages.quote: Sages look with an equal eye on a Brahmana endowed with learning and humility, on a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
This truth is equal everywhere; it has no high and no low. That is why it is called supreme, perfect awakening.

O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware
The stranger that sojourneth with you shall be unto you as the home-born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.

title: Give Without Keeping Score
hook: Is it still generous if you expect something back?
common: Giving is praised everywhere — and so is giving without wanting thanks, credit or return.
differ: The Torah and Bible speak of God seeing and blessing the giver; the Quran frames it as giving 'for the sake of Allah only'; the Gita classifies gifts by the giver's intention; the Diamond Sutra asks the giver to let go even of the idea of giving.
reflect: What would you give today if nobody could ever find out it was you?

passages.quote: That gift which is given to one who does nothing in return, knowing it to be a duty to give in a suitable place and time to a worthy person, is held to be Sattvic.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

A bodhisattva should give without clinging to anything — giving without attachment to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touch or ideas. If one gives without clinging to appearances, the merit is beyond measure, like the boundless space in every direction.
And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you

Thou shalt surely give him, and thy heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him; because that for this thing the LORD thy God will bless thee in all thy work, and in all that thou puttest thy hand unto. For the poor shall never cease out of the land; therefore I command thee, saying: ‘Thou shalt surely open thy hand unto thy poor and needy brother, in thy land.’

title: Answer Harm With Good
hook: What do you owe someone who hurt you?
common: None of the five treat revenge as the ideal. Each points toward help, goodwill or freedom from hatred — even toward an opponent.
differ: The Torah gives a concrete case (help your enemy's struggling animal); Jesus says to love and pray for enemies; the Quran says to repel evil with something better; the Gita describes the ideal person as hating no creature; the Diamond Sutra tells of staying free of anger while being harmed. All five also contain teachings about justice and self-defence, so read them in context.
reflect: Is there someone you could do one small good thing for, even though you're not okay with them?

passages.quote: He who hates no creature, is friendly and compassionate to all, is free from attachment and egoism, is balanced in pleasure and pain, and is forgiving. Ever content, steady in meditation, self-controlled, possessing firm conviction, with the mind and intellect dedicated to Me, he, My devotee, is dear to Me.

But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.

Long ago, when the King of Kalinga cut my body apart, I had no idea of a self, a person, a being or a life. If I had held on to those ideas while my limbs were being cut off, anger and hatred would have arisen in me.
The good deed and the evil deed are not alike. Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend

If thou meet thine enemy’s ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again. If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under its burden, thou shalt forbear to pass by him; thou shalt surely release it with him.

title: Forgive
hook: Is forgiving the same as forgetting?
common: Forgiveness shows up as a quality of the Divine, a duty for people, or both.
differ: In the Torah, God's mercy sits side by side with justice that 'will by no means clear the guilty'. Jesus links being forgiven to forgiving others; the Quran does too, asking the generous to pardon. The Gita lists forgiveness among 'divine' qualities of character. The Diamond Sutra doesn't discuss forgiveness directly — its focus is on not creating the resentment in the first place (see 'Answer Harm With Good').
reflect: What would change for you if you let one grudge go this week?

passages.quote: Vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of hatred, absence of pride—these belong to one born for a divine state, O Arjuna.
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

passages.none: No close parallel in the Diamond Sutra. That's a real difference worth noticing, not a gap to paper over.

passages.quote: And let not those who possess dignity and ease among you swear not to give to the near of kin and to the needy, and to fugitives for the cause of Allah. Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed: ‘The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth; keeping mercy unto the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children’s children, unto the third and unto the fourth generation.’

title: Stay Humble
hook: Who actually did the thing you're proud of?
common: Every text warns against pride and against taking full credit for your own success.
differ: The Torah and Quran point you back to God as the source; the Bible promises a reversal where the humble are lifted; the Gita says ego mistakes itself for the doer; the Diamond Sutra says even thinking 'I have attained' is a trap.
reflect: Name one person or thing that made your last win possible.

passages.quote: All actions are wrought in all cases by the qualities of Nature alone. He whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Subhūti said: If an arhat were to think, 'I have attained arhatship,' he would be holding on to a self, a person, a being and a life. World-Honoured One, I do not think, 'I am an arhat free from desire.'
The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace

and thou say in thy heart: ‘My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth.’ But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is He that giveth thee power to get wealth, that He may establish His covenant which He swore unto thy fathers, as it is this day.

title: Speak the Truth
common: Honesty is a basic expectation in all five.
differ: The Torah lists lying alongside stealing; the Bible grounds honesty in belonging to one another; the Quran warns against mixing truth with falsehood or hiding it; the Gita adds that truthful speech should also be kind and helpful; the Diamond Sutra describes the Awakened One as someone who never deceives.
reflect: Is there something true you've been avoiding saying?

passages.quote: Speech that causes no excitement, is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial; the practice of studying the Vedas is called austerity of speech.
Therefore putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor. For we are members of one another.
The Tathāgata speaks what is true, what is real, what is as it is. He does not deceive, and he does not say otherwise.
Confound not truth with falsehood, nor knowingly conceal the truth
Ye shall not steal; neither shall ye deal falsely, nor lie one to another.

title: Finding Inner Peace
hook: Where does peace actually come from?
common: Peace is offered as something deeper than circumstances going well.
differ: In the Torah it is a blessing received from God; Jesus offers a peace 'not as the world gives'; the Quran finds rest for the heart in remembering God; the Gita finds it in letting go of craving; the Diamond Sutra in a mind that 'dwells nowhere' — not grabbing onto anything.
reflect: What's one thing you're gripping tightly that you could loosen today?

passages.quote: He attains peace into whom all desires enter, just as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires. That person attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of ownership, and without egoism.
Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.
A bodhisattva should give rise to a pure mind that does not dwell on sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touch or ideas. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
Who have believed and whose hearts have rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest
The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.

title: Don't Cling
hook: Do you own your stuff, or does it own you?
common: All five warn that grasping — for things, results or even ideas — pulls you off course.
differ: The Torah forbids coveting what belongs to others; the Bible contrasts earthly and heavenly treasure; the Quran asks for calm in both loss and gain; the Gita asks you to act fully while releasing the outcome; the Diamond Sutra says even its own teaching is a raft to be left behind once you've crossed.
reflect: What result are you so attached to that it's stressing you out?

passages.quote: Your right is only to work, but not to its results; do not let the results of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure; evenness of mind is called Yoga.

“Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Know that my teaching is like a raft. Even the teaching must be let go of — how much more what is not the teaching.
That ye grieve not for the sake of that which hath escaped you, nor yet exult because of that which hath been given. Allah loveth not all prideful boasters
Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house; thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his man-servant, nor his maid-servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.

title: Everything Passes
common: Each text is clear that bodies, feelings and the world as we see it do not last.
differ: What they say remains is different: the Torah reminds us we return to dust; the Bible and Quran point to what is eternal — the unseen, the 'Countenance of thy Lord'; the Gita says endure the passing and know the Self; the Diamond Sutra asks you simply to see all conditioned things as a dream or a flash of lightning.
reflect: If this worry won't matter in five years, how much energy should it get today?

passages.quote: The contact of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which causes heat and cold, pleasure and pain, has a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them bravely, O Arjuna.
while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; like dew, or a flash of lightning. See them in this way.
Everyone that is thereon will pass away There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken; for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.’

title: Beyond Appearances
common: All five warn against confusing the ultimate with something you can see or picture.
differ: For the Torah, Bible and Quran this is about a personal God who has no visible form. The Gita speaks of an Unmanifest reality behind all forms. The Diamond Sutra, which doesn't teach a creator God, says all appearances are illusory — and seeing that is seeing the Awakened One.
reflect: What image of 'God' or 'the sacred' did you grow up with? Where did it come from?

passages.quote: The foolish think of Me, the Unmanifest, as having manifestation, not knowing My higher, immutable, and most excellent nature.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”
All appearances are illusory. If you see that all appearances are not appearances, then you see the Tathāgata.
Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision. He is the Subtile, the Aware
And the LORD spoke unto you out of the midst of the fire; ye heard the voice of words, but ye saw no form; only a voice.

title: Life, Death and After
common: Every tradition takes death seriously and says how you live now matters.
differ: This is where the texts differ most. The Torah passage stresses choosing life here and now; the Bible centres on resurrection through Jesus; the Quran on a Day of Judgement and paradise; the Gita on an eternal Self taking new bodies; the Diamond Sutra doesn't address the afterlife directly and instead questions the idea of a lasting self at all.
reflect: What do you actually believe happens after death — and what shaped that belief?

passages.quote: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so too the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

passages.none: The Diamond Sutra doesn't describe an afterlife. Its concern is seeing through the idea of a fixed self. It's a genuine difference, so it's left blank.

passages.quote: Every soul will taste of death. And ye will be paid on the Day of Resurrection only that which ye have fairly earned. Whoso is removed from the Fire and is made to enter paradise, he indeed is triumphant. The life of this world is but comfort of illusion
I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before thee life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life, that thou mayest live, thou and thy seed;
